| [LIT-367](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-367.md) v2 | Calculation of signal detection theory measures | Stanislaw & Todorov (1999), DOI-10.3758/BF03207704. A practical tutorial that gives closed-form SDT measures computed from the hit rate H and false-alarm rate F. They are d′ = Φ⁻¹(H) − Φ⁻¹(F); β = exp{[Φ⁻¹(F)² − Φ⁻¹(H)²]/2}; c = −[Φ⁻¹(H) + Φ⁻¹(F)]/2; the nonparametric A′ and Grier's B″ (single-formula versions, eqs. 3 and 9); A_z = Φ(intercept/√(1+slope²)) from the z-ROC, whose slope is σ_noise/σ_signal; and A_d′ = Φ(d′/√2), which equals 2AFC proportion correct under the d′ assumptions. It also gives one-line commands for seven software packages. Its worked rating example (50 signal and 25 noise trials, noise SD larger than signal SD) shows d′ ranging from 0.84 to 1.86 across criteria. | [LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md) | A Network Theory of Mental Disorders | Borsboom (2017), World Psychiatry 16(1):5–13. Mental disorders are not common causes of their symptoms but states of networks of symptoms that cause one another, through "myriads of biological, psychological and societal mechanisms". Five principles; the dynamic one is hysteresis: a strongly connected network, once activated by an external trigger, can sustain itself after the trigger is gone. Disorder is an alternative stable state of a strongly connected network, mental health the stable state of a weakly connected one. Comorbidity follows from bridge symptoms. Treatments are symptom, external-field or network interventions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-435](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-435.md)); worth reading as the short, citable statement of the network theory of mental disorders by its main author. Five principles: disorders are complex systems of interacting components, the components are the symptoms of the diagnostic manuals, the network comes from direct causal connections between symptoms, disorders are the tightly connected clusters, and disorders arise through hysteresis, so a strongly connected network can stay "stuck" after its trigger is gone. Mental health, disorder, resilience and vulnerability are redefined as stable states and dispositions of weakly or strongly connected networks. Its evidence is indirect and it says so: the theory is offered as an "organizing framework" and a deliberate simplification, and the strict symptom-component correspondence of principle 2 is its own flagged weak point. |

| [LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md) | The Diffusion Decision Model: Theory and Data for Two-Choice Decision Tasks | Ratcliff & McKoon (2008), Neural Computation 20(4):873–922. A review of the diffusion decision model for fast two-choice tasks, with three new motion-discrimination experiments. Noisy evidence accumulates from a starting point z to one of two boundaries (0, a) at drift v, plus non-decision time and across-trial variability in v, z and Ter. Two-choice RT and accuracy are decomposed into drift rate (quality of evidence), boundary separation (caution), starting point (bias) and non-decision time, plus across-trial variability in drift, starting point and non-decision time. Three new motion-discrimination experiments show each manipulation landing on its own parameter: difficulty on drift, speed–accuracy instructions on boundaries, stimulus proportion mainly on starting point. | [LIT-609](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-609.md) | Bayesian hypothesis testing for psychologists: A tutorial on the Savage–Dickey method | Wagenmakers, Lodewyckx, Kuriyal & Grasman (2010), Cognitive Psychology 60(3):158–189. For nested models, H0: φ = φ0 inside H1, the Bayes factor BF01 equals the ratio of the posterior to the prior density of φ at φ0 under H1 (Eq. 12), if the nuisance parameters' prior under H1 tends to their prior under H0 as φ → φ0. So a Bayes factor can be read off MCMC samples from the larger model alone, with a nonparametric density estimate at one point. Order restrictions are handled by truncating prior and posterior. Three worked psychology examples, including hierarchical one- and two-sample t-tests. | [LIT-1196](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1196.md) v2 | Self-generated validity and other effects of measurement on belief, attitude, intention, and behavior | Feldman & Lynch (1988). A theoretical paper, with no data of its own. Belief, attitude or intention can be created by measurement when the construct does not already exist in long-term memory, and the created answer is stored and retrieved as an input to later answers and to behaviour. Even when it exists, question order and format decide which earlier answer is used: an earlier response is used for a later one if it is accessible and perceived as more diagnostic than other accessible inputs. Expertise, direct experience and trait involvement reduce the effects, because they supply judgements already formed and rehearsed. | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-957](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-957.md)) in full, from a scan of the published article posted on a University of Florida course page; worth reading as the theoretical statement that a survey question can create the cognition it asks about, which is then stored and retrieved as an input to later answers and to behaviour, with accessibility and perceived diagnosticity deciding which earlier answer is used. Read it knowing that it reports no data of its own and calls itself speculative; that the created state it cares most about is one that drives behaviour; and that the moderators it names (expertise, direct experience, trait involvement) work by supplying judgements already formed and rehearsed, not evidence from outside them. |

Twenty undergraduates (after 12 pre-registered exclusions) who had never taken part in it were shown a text and a video of the procedure and rated how far they expected to feel each of Botvinick & Cohen's three illusion and six control statements, under synchronous and asynchronous brushing. The controls therefore do not match expectations, and the author concludes the illusion "may be, partially or entirely, a suggestion effect"; he proposes controls matched on expectancy and on suggestion difficulty. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1005](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1005.md)) from the author's final manuscript on PsyArXiv; worth reading as the direct test of the assumption behind every standard check on the rubber hand illusion, that expectations are matched between the "illusion" and "control" statements and between synchronous and asynchronous brushing. Twenty people who never underwent the illusion read a description of it, watched a 62-second video and rated, for each of Botvinick & Cohen's nine statements, how far they expected to feel it. They expected the illusion statements more than the control statements under synchrony (1.7 against 0.0, d = 1.40) and the illusion statements more under synchrony than asynchrony (1.7 against 0.4, d = 1.05): the pattern published reports show. Read it as showing that the usual controls cannot rule out suggestion, not as showing that the illusion is suggestion; the author says so. Small, pre-registered, sequential Bayesian stopping, one online sample of undergraduates, and no illusion or drift measured. |

A resampling study of the synchronous-condition reports of 351 participants from Lush et al. 2020, run as 10,000 simulated experiments of 20 participants each. Unselected samples found mean agreement with the three standard statements significantly above zero in 83% of experiments; samples from above the median of hypnotisability (subjective SWASH) in 99%; from below it in 51%. For the ownership statement alone the lower half gave significant agreement in about 4% of experiments, and the upper half in 74% (supplement). The authors argue that the relationship is not too small to matter, that the synchronous–asynchronous difference cannot be interpreted because of Lush (2020), and that implicit, neuroimaging and animal measures are tied to ownership only through these reports. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1001](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1001.md)) from the accepted manuscript on PsyArXiv, with the authors' analysis notebooks for 10, 20 and 50 participants; worth reading as the clearest demonstration of what a modest correlation between hypnotisability and rubber hand report does to a field of small studies. Resampling the 351 synchronous-condition reports of Lush et al. 2020 in simulated experiments of 20, samples drawn from the upper half of the hypnotisability scale found significant agreement with the three illusion statements 99% of the time and samples from the lower half 51%; for the one ownership statement, "I felt as if the rubber hand were my hand", the figures were 74% and 4%. Read it as a reanalysis of one dataset, with no new data and no asynchronous or drift analysis. | [LIT-1281](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1281.md) | The Rubber Hand Illusion: Feeling of Ownership and Proprioceptive Drift Do Not Go Hand in Hand | Rohde, Di Luca & Ernst (2011), PLoS ONE 6:e21659. Robot arms stroked a rubber hand and the hidden real hand, and felt finger position was probed by a projected dot. Drift toward the rubber hand built up to about 5–6 cm under synchronous stroking, and to the same level when the hand was only seen, unstroked, or when asynchronous stroking was interrupted every 10 s for measurement. Only 120 s of continuous asynchronous stroking held drift near zero (about 1 cm), which reproduces the classic synchronous–asynchronous difference. The questionnaire showed ownership only after synchronous stroking. The authors conclude that drift and ownership come from different integration processes, that asynchrony suppresses drift rather than synchrony causing it, and that drift is not a valid proxy for ownership. Groups were of ten. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1009](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1009.md)) in full; worth reading as the study that broke the assumed tie between proprioceptive drift and the feeling of owning the rubber hand. With robot-delivered stroking and a visual probe of felt finger position, drift toward the rubber hand appeared under synchronous stroking, under no stroking at all (only seeing the hand), and under asynchronous stroking interrupted every 10 s, at levels not significantly different from synchronous stroking (about 5–6 cm); only continuous asynchronous stroking kept it near zero. Ownership, by questionnaire, needed synchrony. The authors conclude that drift comes from visuo-proprioceptive integration that asynchrony suppresses, and that "conclusions about feelings of ownership cannot be drawn from measuring proprioceptive drift alone". Read it as groups of 10, a visual-judgement measure rather than reaching, and an Experiment 2 whose ownership evidence is anecdotal debriefing, not a questionnaire. |
| [LIT-1387](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1387.md) v2 | Doorways do not always cause forgetting: a multimodal investigation | McFadyen et al. (2021). Four experiments, in immersive virtual reality with and without a working-memory load, in passive video and in real movement, found no significant effect of doorways on forgetting; under working-memory load, false alarms to mismatched probes rose after a doorway. The authors question the effect's robustness to small changes of paradigm. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1079](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1079.md)) from the publisher's text in PubMed Central (PMC7938580, CC BY 4.0); worth holding as the record's only test of the doorway effect outside the originating lab: in passive head-mounted VR doorways did not lower hits (Bayes factors 3–6 for the null), under a counting load they raised false alarms to recombined probes, and a curtained hallway, watched or walked, did not affect memory for a 16-item arrangement. | [LIT-1436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1436.md) | Toward an integrative psychometric model of emotions | Lange, Dalege, Borsboom, van Kleef & Fischer (2020), Perspectives on Psychological Science 15(2):444–468. An integrative psychometric model of emotions must allow distinct emotions (affect-program theories), variation between and within persons (constructionist theories) and causal relations among components (appraisal theories). Reflective and formative latent-variable models do not; a psychometric network model, in which "the network constitutes the emotion", does. Distinct emotions are weakly emergent small-world communities of components. Strongly connected networks sustain their own activation, which predicts hysteresis and longer emotions. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1098](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1098.md)): in part, from the published version (CC BY-NC) deposited in the University of Amsterdam's repository. Worth reading as the proposal that an emotion is a network of causally interacting components, the move Borsboom made for mental disorders ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) applied to emotion. Affect-program, constructionist and appraisal theories each demand one property: distinct emotions, variation between and within persons, and causal relations among components. Reflective and formative latent-variable models fail at least one. A network model meets all three, with a distinct emotion as a weakly emergent small-world community. Strong connectivity predicts self-sustaining activation and hysteresis, so longer emotions. The persistence it gives is a network state's, not an ordering's, and the model is unsigned. |

| [LIT-1440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1440.md) | Induction and Profiling of Strong Multi-Componential Emotions in Virtual Reality | Meuleman & Rudrauf (2021), IEEE Trans. Affective Computing 12:189–202 (online 2018). Passive induction yields weak emotions that do not engage all components, so componential hypotheses cannot be tested with it. In VR, 53 participants played seven games (154 balanced observations) and rated componential items after each. Item clustering gave fear and joy clusters spanning appraisal, motivation, physiology, feeling and regulation. Appraisal predicted fear and joy intensity best. Game differences in fear were absorbed by appraisal and regulation, subject differences in joy were not. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1097](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1097.md)): in full, from the authors' accepted manuscript in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:112041). Worth reading as an argument, with data, that passive induction (pictures, film) cannot test componential hypotheses such as synchronization, because it does not engage all components, and that virtual reality can. 53 participants played seven commercial VR games and rated appraisal, motivation, physiology, feeling and regulation items after each. Clustering found multi-componential fear and joy patterns, and appraisal items predicted fear and joy intensity best. Componentiality is assessed across observations, one retrospective self-report per game. Nothing is measured within an episode, and there is no synchronization index. |
| [LIT-1443](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1443.md) | A Multi-Componential Approach to Emotion Recognition and the Effect of Personality | Mohammadi & Vuilleumier (2022), IEEE Trans. Affective Computing 13:1127–1139 (online 2020). Crowdworkers rated 39 CoreGRID items and 10 discrete emotions after watching film clips (1,567 surveys, 99 clips). Clustering of emotion profiles in componential space separates positive from negative, then five clusters. PCA gives six dimensions beyond valence and arousal. Ordinal regression on all components predicts discrete-emotion ratings best; no single component suffices. Personality correlates more with componential items than with feelings or discrete emotions. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1118](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1118.md)): in full, from the authors' arXiv preprint (2010.11370v1, October 2020). | [LIT-1444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1444.md) | Brain networks subserving functional core processes of emotions identified with componential modeling | Mohammadi, Van De Ville & Vuilleumier (2023), Cerebral Cortex 33:7993–8010. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and rated 119 salient events (12 s each) on 32 CoreGRID features, and heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation between event-wise brain maps and feature ratings yields six latent variables, the "functional core processes": valuation (wanting-like), novelty, hedonic impact (liking-like), goal monitoring, caring for others ("being moved") and approach/avoidance. No arousal process emerges, and the processes mix components rather than mapping one to one. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1107](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1107.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:170302). Worth reading as the first attempt to recover the component process model's components from brain and behaviour together. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and then rated 119 salient 12-second events on 32 CoreGRID features. Heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation found six brain–behaviour latent variables, read as valuation, novelty, hedonic impact, goal monitoring, caring for others and approach/avoidance. For the record, the result is two distinct valence-like networks: a "wanting"-like valuation process and a "liking"-like hedonic one. Each event gets a feature vector, but no within-episode synchronization is computed. |
| [LIT-1448](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1448.md) | Back to Bentham? Explorations of Experienced Utility | Kahneman, Wakker & Sarin (1997), Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(2):375–405. "Utility" has two meanings: decision utility, an outcome's weight in choice, and experienced utility, its hedonic quality. Experienced utility is instant (the pleasure or distress of the moment, reported in real time) or remembered (a retrospective evaluation). Remembered utility follows the Peak-End average and neglects duration. Choices follow remembered utility, so subjects repeat a longer cold-water trial that dominates the shorter one in pain. Axioms on ordinal instant utility with a neutral zero make total utility the time integral of a value transform. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1105](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1105.md)): in full, from the published article as deposited in Erasmus University Rotterdam's repository (RePub, hdl 1765/23011). Distinguishes decision utility (an outcome's weight in choice) from experienced utility (hedonic quality). Experienced utility divides into instant utility, reported in real time, and remembered utility, a retrospective evaluation. Remembered utility follows a Peak-End rule and neglects duration. Choices follow remembered utility, so people choose dominated, longer painful episodes. Axioms on ordinal instant utility with a neutral zero yield total utility as a time integral. Filed for the record's three-layer operationalization of felt valence ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)). |

Worth reading as the one study here that tests whether appraisal acts on the other emotion components linearly. It re-analyses the GRID data, culturally shared semantic profiles of 24 emotion words rated in 34 samples from 27 countries. It fits multivariate adaptive regression splines from seven appraisal factors to eleven motivation, physiology and expression factors. Goal compatibility is the main effect. Agency and norm compatibility act only in interactions, and some responses need splines. Its "threshold effects" are hinges in a continuous piecewise-linear fit.
